Access state: the lakecountyfl.gov estate answers HTTP 403 behind a Cloudflare managed challenge

Challenged hosts: www.lakecountyfl.gov, c.lakecountyfl.gov, gis.lakecountyfl.gov.
Evidence: HTTP 403 with server cloudflare and cf-mitigated challenge on every path.
Consequence: Permit detail pages carrying contractor of record cannot be fetched.
The CD Plus permit data is still readable because the Esri MapServer proxy is vendor-hosted on utility.arcgis.com and does not sit behind that estate. It is the permit detail pages, not the permit records, that are blocked.
This single access state is what removes contractor of record from the published dataset.

chunks.title: Cost model — why Oracle carries no ongoing infrastructure cost — Cost model — why Oracle carries no ongoing infrastructure cost › The read path
headingPath: Cost model — why Oracle carries no ongoing infrastructure cost
The read path
chunks.textForEmbedding:
Cost model — why Oracle carries no ongoing infrastructure cost > Cost model — why Oracle carries no ongoing infrastructure cost > The read path

Published data lives on IPFS as immutable CIDs. A consumer resolves a CID through any
public gateway, or through their own IPFS node, and gets the bytes. The query surface is a
20 MB Parquet file that DuckDB reads with HTTP range requests, so a browser can answer
"which properties within five miles have roofs older than fifteen years" by fetching a few
kilobytes of the relevant column chunks — no database, no API server, no compute owned by
Oracle.

| Component | Who runs it | Ongoing cost to Oracle |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------- |
| Published dataset | Public IPFS | none |
| Pinning | Filebase free plan | none at this volume |
| Query engine | DuckDB in the consumer's browser or process | none |
| MCP server | Whoever wants one; it is stateless and reads the public CIDs | none |
| Ingestion | A laptop or a scheduled runner, minutes per run | none between runs |

Delete every account involved and the dataset still resolves: `artifacts/manifest-<run>.json`
lists each artifact's CID, byte size and SHA-256, and the CAR file rebuilds the whole DAG on
any IPFS node without re-encoding it.

What ingestion actually costs
chunks.textForEmbedding:
Cost model — why Oracle carries no ongoing infrastructure cost > Cost model — why Oracle carries no ongoing infrastructure cost > What ingestion actually costs

The full county acquires in well under a minute of network time and consolidates in about
two seconds. There is no scraping fleet because there is nothing to scrape: every source is
a bulk download or a bounded Esri page walk.

| Stage | Measured |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| DOR NAL + SDF + TPP download | 42 s |
| GIO centroids, 210,935 rows | ~10 s at concurrency 4 |
| CD Plus permits, 17,915 features | 6.5 s |
| Seed build, 215,806 rows | 7.4 s |
| Query-table consolidation in DuckDB | 2.2 s |
| Publish-set build (22 shards, samples, schema, coverage) | 15 s |

Ingestion is therefore free on any machine that already exists, and an incremental refresh
is cheaper still: the permit layer is windowed on `Permit_LastModDate`, so a daily run
fetches only what moved.

chunks.textForEmbedding:
Kit deviations — where Lake County departs from the team kit and why > Lake County — deviations from the team kit, and why > 11. Two honest inefficiencies, named rather than hidden

**Every run re-uploads the whole DAG.** The published run directory is ~312 MB, dominated by
the 22 property shards, and an incremental run currently uploads a CAR containing all of it
even when only a few hundred permits moved. IPFS blocks are content-addressed, so the
unchanged blocks are already pinned and a CAR carrying only the new blocks plus the new root
path would be enough. That optimisation is identified but not implemented; the current
behaviour is correct, just wasteful of upload time.

**IPNS resolution is not universal across gateways.** `ipfs.filebase.io`, `ipfs.io`,
`dweb.link` and `w3s.link` resolve `/ipns/<name>/…` and return the published files.
`gateway.pinata.cloud` and `gw.ipfs-lens.dev` answer 403 for IPNS paths while serving
`/ipfs/<cid>` paths normally. The hosted runtime therefore resolves the name against the
narrower list and reads the resolved CID from the wider one; both lists are properties of
each gateway in `packages/shared/src/gateways.ts`, measured rather than assumed.

`deploy-open-data-mcp` lists `ORACLE_OPEN_DATA_INDEX_CID` as optional and says to
leave it UNSET when using IPNS, "so IPNS is the single source of truth". That rule

— `artifacts/latest.json`'s `rootCid`, accepted only when `resolvedCid` equals it,

first requests, upgrading when it finds a newer run. That is not a second source of

 configuration the function has.
- The cached value is itself an IPNS resolution, not an alternative to one, and the
 live pointer overrides it as soon as they disagree on a newer run.
- A redeploy is not needed to move it. That is what makes it different from a
 pinned CID; the pin's defining property is that only a deploy can change it.

`county-open-data-publish` and `durable-workflow-builder` pattern 10 put the human

writing anything — the run's root CID is the content watermark, which is what makes
the throttle exact rather than approximate.

The kit's `.mcp.json` starts the elephant MCP with

GitHub dependency tree on **every** launch, which measured here as:

| --- | --- |
| `npx` from `#main`, cold | 86 s |
| `npx` from `#main`, warm | 38 s |
| `npx` pinned to commit `aad2785`, cold | 190 s |
| `npx` pinned to commit `aad2785`, warm | 119 s |
| Pre-installed binary | **1–2 s** |

when there isn't one:

```sh
if [ -x "$BIN" ]; then exec "$BIN"; fi
exec npx -y --package=github:elephant-xyz/elephant-mcp#main mcp
```

reviewer nothing. To take the fast path:

```sh
npm install --prefix ~/.elephant-mcp github:elephant-xyz/elephant-mcp#main
```

 Key appears in `Alternate_Key`. The Alternate Key is the better join: it is populated on

3. Permit portal
chunks.textForEmbedding:
County profile — Lake County, FL discovery findings > Lake County, FL — county profile > 3. Permit portal

Permits are **not** a county-level dataset here. One county service plus 14 independent
municipal systems.

- **Unincorporated Lake County** — Perconti CD Plus, exposed as an Esri MapServer layer
 through `utility.arcgis.com`. Open, no session, no challenge. 17,915 features, 17,671
 distinct permit numbers, 12,454 distinct parcels, fetched in 6.5 s at concurrency 4.
 `IN (...)` lists longer than about 50 values return HTTP 500, so paging is done by
 OBJECTID range.
- Two measured limits on that layer, both material:
 - **Jurisdiction.** A spatial test of every permit parcel against the 14 Census city
 polygons puts 45 of 17,915 features (0.25%) inside any city limit, and those are Lake
 County government facilities the county permits for itself. Mailing city is not a
 jurisdiction signal: 4,688 features carry a Clermont mailing address while sitting in
 unincorporated south Lake.
 - **Time.** `Permit_LastModDate` spans 2025-09-09 to 2026-09-08 — a 365-day rolling
 window. Only 846 of 17,671 permits (4.8%) were issued before 2024-09-09. This is a
 current-permit service, not a permit archive.
- **The 14 municipalities.** Exactly one, **Clermont**, has an open machine-readable
 portal: CentralSquare eTRAKiT 3, searchable by "AK NUMBER" which is the NAL Alternate
 Key, and its detail pages expose **contractor names** — the very field the county layer
 withholds. The other 13 are blocked by login, captcha, bot protection or TLS failure, or
 have no online search at all. Each has a named records-request route in
 `docs/lake-sources.yaml`.

chunks.textForEmbedding:
Project README — Oracle Property Intelligence Pipeline, Lake County FL > Oracle Property Intelligence Pipeline — Lake County, FL > Architecture

```
bulk sources (no scraping fleet: every source is a download or a bounded Esri page walk)
 ├─ FL DOR NAL / SDF / TPP ── 42 s
 ├─ FL GIO parcel centroids ── 210,935 rows, ids-only + OBJECTID ranges, ~10 s
 └─ Lake CD Plus permits ── 17,915 features, 6.5 s, windowed for incremental runs
 │
 seed ├─ data/seeds/lake.csv, 215,806 rows, no PII, reconciliation enforced
 │
 DuckDB├─ join → 62-column query table → gate: rows == distinct folio, 0 null folios
 │
publish ├─ UnixFS DAG built and hashed LOCALLY → CIDv1 base32 → CAR
 ├─ CAR imported to Filebase with x-amz-meta-import: car, pinning the exact DAG
 ├─ IPNS re-pointed, then READ BACK and compared to the published root
 └─ every listed CID fetched from independent public gateways, bytes and sha256 compared
 │
 read └─ DuckDB range-reads the Parquet by CID. No server in the read path.
```

chunks.textForEmbedding:
Project README — Oracle Property Intelligence Pipeline, Lake County FL > Oracle Property Intelligence Pipeline — Lake County, FL > No single gateway can take this down

Both read paths — the Lambda and the browser — try several gateways for the same
CID and use the first that answers. Pinning one vendor's gateway put the runtime
in tension with this project's own rule that a vendor-specific HTTP URL is never
the source of truth, and made the no-ongoing-cost claim depend on one account
staying live. The CID is the source of truth; a gateway is transport.

Measured against the published Parquet on 2026-09-10, following redirects
(`curl -sL -r 0-1023 -H 'Origin: ...'`), rather than assumed:

| Gateway | Range | CORS | Used |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------- | ----- | ---- | ---------------------------------------- |
| `ipfs.filebase.io` · `gateway.pinata.cloud` · `gw.ipfs-lens.dev` | 206 | `*` | in order |
| `ipfs.io` · `dweb.link` · `w3s.link` | 206 | `*` | last — they rate-limit datacenter egress |
| `4everland.io` | 301 | `*` | recorded unusable, not silently omitted |

The `-L` matters, and a first pass here got it wrong without it: `dweb.link` and
`w3s.link` answer 301 to a subdomain gateway and serve the range from there, so
every real client sees 206. An earlier note in this repo claimed Filebase was the
only gateway serving both CORS and Range; five others do.

Not harvested: an eTRAKiT adapter and a throughput measurement are needed first, and neither was in scope for this run. This is the single most valuable remaining source, because it is the only open route to contractor of record anywhere in the county.

Permit jurisdictions in Lake County, Florida — who issues permits and which ones are blocked

Lake County permitting is not a single countywide system. There are 15 permit-issuing jurisdictions: unincorporated Lake County plus 14 independent municipalities, each running its own building department and its own permit software.
Exactly one jurisdiction is harvested into the published dataset: Unincorporated Lake County, through the Perconti CD Plus permit layer. The other 14 are blocked, unavailable, manual-only, or open but never harvested.
Jurisdictions that are NOT in the published data: Clermont (open portal, not harvested, discovered-open-portal); Groveland (blocked, blocked-login-required); Eustis (blocked, blocked-bot-challenge); Minneola (blocked, blocked-cloudflare-challenge); Leesburg (blocked, blocked-captcha); Tavares (unavailable, unreachable-from-egress); Mount Dora (blocked, blocked-bot-challenge); Umatilla (manual-only, no-public-historical-search); Astatula (manual-only, no-public-historical-search); Fruitland Park (blocked, blocked-bot-challenge); Howey-in-the-Hills (blocked, blocked-captcha); Lady Lake (blocked, blocked-egress-tls-failure); Mascotte (blocked, blocked-captcha); Montverde (manual-only, no-public-historical-search).
Every blocked jurisdiction has a named public-records request recipient in the source catalog, so the records can still be obtained by a Chapter 119 request. Ask for the jurisdiction by name to get its recipient office, request channel and system scope.

First, jurisdiction: a spatial test of every permit parcel against the 14 Census city polygons puts 45 of 17,915 features (0.25%) inside any city limit, and those are Lake County government facilities that the county permits for itself. chunks.title: Data source: Lake County CD Plus permit layer (lake_cdplus_permits)
chunks.textForEmbedding:
Data source: Lake County CD Plus permit layer (lake_cdplus_permits)

The only permit source in the published dataset. 17,915 features, 17,671 distinct permit numbers, 12,454 distinct parcels.
Roofing permits: 3,312. Open permits: 3,753. Open roofing permits: 247.
Join: the permit layer's Alternate_Key matches the NAL ALT_KEY column; the undashed PARCEL_ID matches the layer's Parcel_ID. Alternate_Key is the better join because it is populated on 100% of permit features.
Two measured limits: The county CD Plus layer is NOT a countywide permit archive. Two measured limits. First, jurisdiction: a spatial test of every permit parcel against the 14 Census city polygons puts 45 of 17,915 features (0.25%) inside any city limit, and those are Lake County government facilities that the county permits for itself. The layer is unincorporated Lake County only, and no municipality delegates permitting to the county. Mailing city is not a jurisdiction signal - 4,688 features carry a CLERMONT mailing address while sitting in unincorporated south Lake. Second, time: Permit_LastModDate spans 2025-09-09 to 2026-09-08, exactly a 365-day rolling window, and only 846 of 17,671 permits (4.8%) were issued before 2024-09-09. The layer publishes recently-modified permits, not history.
Contractor of record is NOT exposed by this layer. It lives on the county permit detail pages, which sit behind a Cloudflare managed challenge, so contractor_name is published null.
Endpoint: https://utility.arcgis.com/usrsvcs/servers/365d9a169bc34110a3db2157c76f6c95/rest/services/Individual/CDPermitParcels/MapServer/0. IN lists longer than about 50 values return HTTP 500, so paging is done by OBJECTID range.

chunks.textForEmbedding:
Data source: Florida GIO statewide parcel centroids 2025 (fl_gio_parcel_centroid_2025)

Florida DOR 2026 preliminary NAL is the parcel denominator; geometry comes from the Florida GIO statewide parcel-centroid 2025 FeatureServer, which publishes 210,935 Lake rows.
That is 4,871 fewer than the assessed roll (2.26%), because the centroid release is one roll year older than the 2026 roll.
Why the gap is acceptable: The canonical denominator is the DOR 2026 preliminary NAL (215,806 rows, measured). The geometry source is the Florida GIO statewide parcel-centroid 2025 release (210,935 Lake rows, measured), which is one roll year older, so parcels first assessed for 2026 - new splits, new condo units and new construction - have no 2025 centroid yet. Geometry is never used as the parcel denominator and never seeds a parcel; it only decorates a NAL row that already exists.
Consequence for the query table: latitude and longitude are null for parcels first assessed in 2026. Those rows are published with null coordinates rather than dropped, so a radius search silently excludes them unless requireCoordinates is understood.
Endpoint: https://services9.arcgis.com/Gh9awoU677aKree0/arcgis/rest/services/Florida_Statewide_Parcel_Centroid_Version/FeatureServer/0. Offset paging breaks past 20,000 rows, so the fetch uses ids-only plus OBJECTID ranges.

chunks.title: Data source: Florida DOR NAL 2026 preliminary tax roll (fl_dor_nal_2026p)
chunks.textForEmbedding:
Data source: Florida DOR NAL 2026 preliminary tax roll (fl_dor_nal_2026p)

The NAL roll is the canonical parcel source and the denominator for every coverage claim: 215,806 assessed parcels in Lake County.
It supplies address, owner name and mailing address, property and usage type, DOR use code, year built, livable area, building count, assessed / market / land / taxable value, and the two most recent sales carried on the roll.
Measured field coverage: year built known on 169,007 parcels, physical ZIP on 212,737, owner name on 215,620, 168,315 distinct owner names, 20,236 out-of-state owners.
Identifier: DOR Parcel ID (with Alternate Key as the permit join), format NN-NN-NN-NNNN-NNN-NNNNN (23 characters); ALT_KEY is 7 digits. Join rule: PARCEL_ID and ALT_KEY are both unique across all 215,806 NAL rows (measured: 215,806 distinct of each). ALT_KEY joins the CD Plus permit layer's Alternate_Key; the undashed PARCEL_ID matches the layer's Parcel_ID.
Limitation: only the current roll is published. There is no attribute-bearing historical roll before 2024F, so nothing on this source can prove ownership history.
Bulk download portal: https://floridarevenue.com/property/dataportal.

chunks.textForEmbedding:
Data source: Florida DOR SDF 2026 preliminary sales file (fl_dor_sdf_2026p)

Florida DOR SDF 2026 preliminary plus NAL SALE_YR1/SALE_YR2. 37,020 sale records covering 30,977 parcels.
Sale window published: 2025 to 2026 only.
Ten-year ownership tenure provable from published sources: NO.
Evidence: Only the current roll is published: the NAL folder exposes 2026P alone, and both SDF and NAL SALE_YR1 span 2025-2026 only. The DOR Map Data archive publishes Lake parcel files back to 2005F, but they carry parcel geometry only - the 2010 Lake file was downloaded and its attribute table holds exactly two fields, CO_NO and PARCEL_ID, across 178,377 records. Attribute-bearing PAR files begin at 2024F. Ownership tenure beyond the 2025-2026 window therefore cannot be proven from any published Lake source. The query table exposes no_recorded_sale_in_dor_window as an explicit lower bound and never claims a tenure length.
Consequence for the query table: no_recorded_sale_in_dor_window is a lower bound on tenure, never a tenure length. A property with no sale in the window may have changed hands in 2019 and the published data cannot tell.
